1:
Three voices object to the chapter division. Adam Clarke says it has interrupted the discourse and broken it off almost mid-sentence; Charles Ellicott calls the separation wrong and makes the verse the climax of the chastisement of the daughters of Zion; John Calvin says it ought not to have been parted from what precedes, the description filling out the calamity already threatened so that hypocrites may not palliate the warning.

Matthew Henry begins from the arithmetic: providence has ordered that nearly equal numbers of men and women are born, but war can leave scarcely one man in seven alive, and as there are deaths peculiar to women in childbirth, so there are deaths peculiar to men by the sword, which perhaps devour more. He lists three reversals: men ordinarily make their court to the women, whereas here the women take hold of the men, fearing as Lot’s daughters did at the ruin of Sodom that none was left; women naturally hate to be sharers, yet seven now consent to one husband; and where the law obliged a husband to provide food and clothing, these women bind themselves to earn it. Clarke adds the motive, that they beg only the name and credit of wedlock and freedom from the reproach of celibacy, and sets beside it a Roman woman’s plea in a poem for the empty name of marriage.

Ellicott sharpens the reversal by looking back a chapter: as men there sought a protector in vain, so women here seek a husband, those who had been wooed and were proudly fastidious now supplicating in rivalry, the seven to one implying a land depopulated by war. He corrects the last clause, which he would read as an imperative, take thou away, and identifies the reproach as childlessness, from the Jewish standpoint not only the great sorrow of womanhood but its great shame, implying a sin that it punished. John Wesley agrees that virginity was counted a reproach, children being an honour to parents and a blessing of God.

The date is disputed. John Gill rejects the dating in the days of Ahaz, since two hundred thousand women were carried captive at that same slaughter, and refers the verse to the wars of the Roman emperors with the Jews, when there were not men enough for every woman to have a husband; he reports a rabbinic tradition that a conqueror had forbidden his army to marry another man’s wife, but says the time does not fit. Clarke notes that the opening words are absent from the Greek version and from manuscripts.

The second verse turns the chapter round, and the readings part. Henry says the sun breaks out from behind the cloud, and takes the branch as one of the prophetical names of Christ, planted by God’s power and flourishing to his praise, the ancient paraphrase reading it as the Messiah of the Lord. Gill rejects the readings that make it the wise men left among the people, or the reforming king, and settles on the Messiah; Clarke and Wesley agree, Clarke taking the fruit of the land for the person to spring from the house of Judah. Ellicott goes furthest, calling this the first distinct prophecy in the book of a personal Messiah, noting that later prophets took both thought and word from this passage, and dismissing the reading that takes the branch collectively for vegetation. Calvin holds precisely that rejected view. He grants the Messianic exposition is plausible, supported by a later prophet and by the respectful title given here; but after examining the whole he makes both phrases denote an unusual and abundant supply of grace to relieve the hungry, the barren land’s sudden fertility making God’s kindness the more welcome. Keil and Delitzsch supply the logic: the judgment was itself the medium of salvation, since a city judged would be sifted, and by being sifted rescued, pardoned and glorified.
3:
Keil and Delitzsch put the weight of the third verse on one word. Where formerly people had been distinguished by rank without regard to moral worth, holy would now become the one chief title of honour and belong to every individual; and shall be called, they note, is not simply equivalent to shall be but presupposes it, the term meaning what is separated from the world. Charles Ellicott draws the contrast historically, the prophet turning from the city that then was, with its hypocrisies and harlot fashions, to a new one in which everyone should be called holy and the name should be no mockery but express the self-consecration of the inhabitants. John Wesley compresses it: they shall be really holy.

The register divides them. Ellicott takes the phrase literally as for life and identifies it with the book of life, in which are written the names of those worthy of the heavenly city; examining the places where it occurs, he concludes that while the image involves an election it excludes an irreversible predestination, the election having to be made sure by a life in harmony with it. John Gill finds the exact opposite here, the doctrine of the final perseverance of the saints, with their sanctification and election secured in the clauses that follow. John Calvin objects to a third reading, that those written in the book of life shall be holy, as too limited, and keeps the clauses separate, such repetition being frequent when the same gift is set out under various titles. Adam Clarke keeps the phrase administrative: it means whose name stands in the enrolment of the people, registering being agreeable to the law and useful in policy.

The washing of the fourth verse is two operations. Keil and Delitzsch match the double purification to the two scenes of judgment in the previous chapter, take the filth of the daughters for the moral pollution hidden under their coquettish finery, and render the second phrase spirit of sifting rather than of burning. Ellicott makes the link back explicit, since the prophet has not forgotten the daughters of Zion, and distinguishes the two evils by their remedies: the uncleanness beneath the show of beauty could be washed away as with a baptism of repentance, whereas the bloodshed, ranging from murders to sacrifices in which the women had borne a conspicuous part, needed the fiery baptism of wrath. He prefers the more literal breath or blast for spirit, and notes that burning is used elsewhere of destruction generally.

Clarke turns the fire into metallurgy: it is the fire of God’s wrath, gathering the people into a furnace to separate dross from silver, as two other prophets have it. The whole alludes to a chemist, who judges the state of the adulterated ore, kindles the proper degree of fire, applies the test, and parts the precious from the vile.

Calvin uses the verse against a common assumption. Because calamities that reduce the church are generally believed to injure her, the prophet urges the contrary, that this is the very method by which God washes away her filth. He reads the blood as covering not murders only but defilements of every kind, calls the clauses a reduplication saying one thing twice, and draws the fruit: our spots are washed away by chastisement, and where abounding iniquity goes unpunished we are corrupted along with everyone else, so that God must warn us in earnest. He observes too that the purification is the Spirit’s work, and that the Spirit takes his names here from the effects he produces. Wesley reads the two names the same way, judgment because the Spirit executes it in the church and in the consciences of men, separating the precious from the vile, and burning because he consumes the dross and inflames believers with love; the burning, he adds, stands opposed to the older legal purification by water.
5:
Charles Ellicott weighs the verb first: create carries all the solemn force it has in the opening sentence of the law, and is one of this prophet’s favourite words. The noun rendered dwelling-place, he adds, is almost always used of the tabernacle or temple, which settles what the assemblies are: not meetings of the people for counsel or debate, as in a Greek city, but solemn gatherings in the temple courts. John Wesley makes the same point about the verb briefly, that God will produce this in a marvellous manner, as it were by a new creation, while John Gill takes each dwelling place for a particular church, the word signifying a place well fitted up and settled.

Keil and Delitzsch read the cloud against the older deliverance and mark what has changed. As God once guided and shielded the people with a cloud by day and a fire by night, which either went before them like a pillar or floated above them as a roof, so he would shield them at the last; but the redeemed would no longer need the pillar, their wanderings being over, and would need only the covering. John Calvin makes the same comparison serve a wider purpose, since it was customary with the prophets, when describing a remarkable blessing, to recall the going out of Egypt, God having then made a display of the boundless treasures of his grace. What chiefly deserved commemorating, he says, was that the cloud protected them from excessive heat by day and went before them by night to keep them from straying; and he warns against pressing the promise literally, since the return from captivity would be as striking as the exodus without a cloud and a fire, God displaying his grace by other methods not less remarkable. Calvin also glosses the second noun as the place where men assemble rather than a proclamation, and sums the verse up in a sentence: there will not be a corner of the mountain on which the grace of God does not shine.

Adam Clarke works the text itself. A manuscript and two versions read he shall bring rather than create, since the cloud already exists and the Lord will bring it over; four manuscripts omit the word all before dwelling place, rightly as it seems to him, the station being the mountain itself and no other; and twenty-five manuscripts give assemblies in the plural. The cloud and smoke he takes for a manifest allusion to the pillar and to the glory that rested on the tabernacle, comparing another prophet’s promise to be a wall of fire round about and a glory in the midst.

The closing verse is shelter. Keil and Delitzsch settle its grammar first, refusing to make the miraculous roofing the subject, since the words disagree in gender and it would make no sense to say that a canopy is a booth; they prefer to take the city itself as the subject, so that Zion becomes a booth, a place of security and concealment. Clarke supplies the object from travel: in countries subject to violent tempests as well as intolerable heat, a portable tent is a necessary part of a traveller’s baggage, and such tents are met with throughout the region. Calvin turns it to consolation and refuses to promise exemption: believers remain exposed to many calamities, and when they escape one danger they meet another, but the protection of the Lord is of itself sufficient against every inconvenience. Good and bad alike suffer, he adds, but the bad have no refuge, whereas the godly have a safe retreat — provided the glory spoken of earlier shines in them, for it is by carrying God’s mark that a man may rest assured of protection. Gill identifies the tabernacle with Christ, who tabernacled in our nature; Wesley reads the clause as saying the Lord himself shall be the shelter.
